newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy central bank chief urges cleanup of finances.
newsitem.headline: Italy central bank chief urges cleanup of finances.

text.p: Central bank governor Antonio Fazio on Saturday urged the Italian government to pursue a clean-up of state finances but warned he would not hesitate to raise interest rates if inflation picked up.
Fazio strongly endorsed the government's three-year economic strategy, unveiled on Friday, which aims to put Italy firmly on course to join a single European currency by 1999.

"We are confident the government and parliament will quickly prepare and use the necessary instruments to give coherences to their objectives," Fazio told the elite of Italian high finance gathered at the Bank of Italy's annual assembly.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday the government planned to slice 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) off the public sector deficit in 1998, combining 15 trillion lire in spending cuts with 10 trillion lire of revenue increases.
The central bank, which has been cautiously lowering interest rates in recent months, was still prepared to increase borrowing costs at the first flicker of inflation, said Fazio.
"We assume that the correction of public spending will continue with clear intent and that inflationary stimuli will not be injected into the economy," he added.
"In the presence of unfavourable developments we will not hesitate to halt our policy of reflation, in extreme cases to change its course," said Fazio.

The government had to be relentless in its efforts to bring down public spending after faltering in the course of 1996. "Despite falling interest rates, the reordering of public accounts came to a halt in 1996," he said.
The economy was set for sluggish growth over the next three years, while Italy engaged in a major struggle to lower public borrowing, but recovery lay ahead if the government succeeded.
"Macroeconomic evaluations indicate unsatisfactory growth for the next three years, unfavourable prospects for jobs growth," said Fazio.
Fazio issued a veiled warning to the government not to impose any increase in the tax burden on the economy, which is already teetering on the brink of recession.
The Prodi government has signalled that it plans to raise revenues by hiking VAT taxes. Fazio said he was also concerned that taxes on consumption could spark inflation.

"It would be an error to try to correct the disequilibria which still remain by acting in a significant way on (tax) revenues, in particularly those which influence the level of prices and costs," said Fazio.
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said on Friday that any increases in VAT would only have a one-off impact on prices and would not be inflationary.
Monetary policy would be subordinated to the aim of keeping inflation below two percent next year.

"The regulation of money and credit, the gradual easing of restrictions will be consistent with this objective," Fazio said, adding the central bank would seek to keep inflation below two percent in 1998.
Inflationary expectations had been beaten down but inflation had not been completely vanquished. "The flames of inflation have not been completely extinguished," he added.
Preliminary data for May show consumer price inflation running at 1.5/1.6 percent year-on-year, its lowest since the late 1960s.
